title: Shinran's family
hookLine: Shinran married and raised a family, neither monk nor layman

lines: A MOTHER'S LETTERS TO HER DAUGHTER.
cards: A box of old letters, kept in a temple archive for a very long time, then read again. They are from a mother to her grown daughter.
She writes about the man she married, how she first understood who he was, what she remembered of his hard years. The man was Shinran. The woman was his wife, Eshinni.

A Buddhist monk with a wife, children, a household and letters home was not the usual picture in his world. Shinran found his own phrase for what he had become: neither monk nor layman. Today, Shinran's family.

teach.h: EXILED, AND NO LONGER A MONK.
teach.b: First, how it happened. When the authorities moved against Honen's community, Shinran was among those sent into exile, and he was stripped of his status as a monk. He never went back to the monastery life.
With his wife, Eshinni, he raised children, and lived among farmers and ordinary people in the provinces, teaching the nembutsu to whoever came. Second, his phrase.
In the closing pages of his major work, the Kyogyoshinsho, he writes of himself that he is therefore neither monk nor layman.
He took the name Gutoku, which carries the sense of a foolish, stubble-haired one: no longer a shaved monk, not quite a layman either. Third, the letters.

Eshinni's letters to their daughter, Kakushinni, are among the ways Shinran can be seen as a person, not only as a teacher. They show a wife who respected him deeply and a family that lived through hard times together.
Fourth, why it matters. Shinran's teaching put all the weight on Amida's vow, not on how pure a life a person could manage.
A married man, raising children, working out the next meal, needed the vow as much as anyone, and could receive it as fully.
In Jodo Shinshu, the school that grew from his teaching, temple priests may marry and raise families, and a temple can also be a family's home.

teach.h: ORDINARY LIFE IS WHERE IT'S WALKED.
teach.b: Ordinary life, in this telling, is not a step down from the path. It is where the path is walked.

how: In Jodo Shinshu, priests may marry, and a local temple may be run by a family who lives on its grounds and serves the community.

o: an order of monks sworn never to marry
Shinran, his wife Eshinni, and their children
the monks who followed Shinran into exile

p: their daughter, who received the letters
where he wrote neither monk nor layman

s: Shinran left Buddhism when he married
he kept teaching the nembutsu, and called himself neither monk nor layman.
letters from his wife Eshinni to their daughter survive
they are among the ways we see Shinran as a person.
Shinran's teaching said only monks could fully receive Amida's vow
he put the weight on the vow, open to a married man as fully as anyone.

games.q: you're Shinran. you've been exiled and stripped of your status as a monk. what do you do next?
o: fight to be restored to the monastery
marry, raise a family, and keep teaching
games.why: Shinran married, raised children, lived among ordinary people, and kept teaching the nembutsu, neither monk nor layman.

practice: Bring to mind the most everyday part of your life, the dishes, the commute, the laundry, the people you live with or call, and choose one.
Hold it in mind without wishing it were something grander, notice the care that is already in it, yours or someone else's, and let a breath or two be a quiet thank you to it.

wordCard.voice: Shinran's family. The teacher who married Eshinni, raised children, and called himself neither monk nor layman. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese hiso hizoku: neither monk nor layman, Shinran's phrase for himself.

carryVoice: Your line: neither monk nor lay. A married man needed the vow as much as anyone. Until tomorrow.
